provenance: the `fast` gate's wall clock went 13s (M2) -> 48.6s (M6) -> 55.4s (M7) -> 67.5s (M8) without one run ever turning red, because ADR-002 Decision 4's 60s ceiling was prose in an ADR and nothing read it. This case has been falsified three times, each one level up from the last, and carries a half for each. (1) It first read `sorted(evals/report/*-fast.json)[-1]`; on the fresh clone `.github/workflows/eval.yml` builds, the newest file is always the report the branch committed, so a tree measuring 77.23s still scored 89/89 = 1.000 with the gate green (PR #20 R1). (2) It then graded `evals.run.over_budget` alone, and the five-line block in `main()` that applies it was pinned by nothing: deleting `evals/run.py`'s `if over_budget(args.suite, totals["wall_seconds"]):` left a 79.02s run — 32% over — reporting 90/90 = 1.000 at exit 0 with this case PASSing (PR #20 R8). Watched red with that block deleted and nothing else touched: `[FAIL] fast-wall-clock-budget`, 89/90 = 0.989 against baseline 1.000, wrong: [{wall_seconds: 79.02, exit: 1, got: 0}] — failing on the run that should have been stopped and not on the one that should not. (3) The ceiling then met CI for the first time and turned out never to have run there: main's own CI does `fast` in 89.62s, ~50% over the same 60s, invisibly. The ceiling became per-environment (ADR-013 Decision 3), so the override is now part of the ruling. Both directions watched red before it existed: with `wall_budget` ignoring the environment, the two positive-value rows fail (`{'env': '95', 'expected_ceiling': 95.0, 'got': 60}`); with an unguarded `float()` that lets garbage mean 'no ceiling', six rows fail (`{'env': None, 'expected_ceiling': 60, 'got': inf}`). The workflow row was red before `.github/workflows/eval.yml` declared anything: `{'workflow': 'EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S', 'declared': None, 'expected': 75}`. (4) And then CI falsified the case one more way, on the run that was supposed to confirm it: it passed locally and failed on CI with `{'suite': 'fast', 'wall_seconds': 70.01, 'over': true}`, because `over_budget` reads the ambient environment and the workflow exports EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S=75 — so 70.01s was correctly not over budget there, and the row asserting otherwise was simply wrong. A case about environment-dependent ceilings that was itself environment-dependent. The rows and the `main()` probes now run with the override cleared, and the fix reproduces both ways: `EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S=75` green, unset green. (5) Round 4 review found the ceiling amendment (60->70) itself was avoidable: `readyz-tracks-the-run-slot`'s `hold_seconds: 3.0` graded the idle->busy->idle transition, not the duration, and ADR-013 Decision 4's claim that 'the sweep above found no third [waste shape]' was false — this was a third one, still in the suite (PR #20 R14). Reduced to `hold_seconds: 2.0` from a margin argument on the actual start-race (submission-to-busy measured at 4.3-5.2ms typically, one 62ms outlier; 2.0s leaves a 0.67s sample gap, ~10x the worst outlier), not copied from the value review happened to measure passing. Recovered ~1.0s per suite run, but a post-fix seven-run band (58.69-60.59s) was published as still straddling 60 on two of seven, so branch 1 (revert to 60) was declared unavailable even after the fix; the published band's slowest run (60.59) fed the same +15%-round-up-to-5 rule to 70s (R15), and `WALL_BUDGET_S` moved to 70. (6) Round 5 review could not reproduce that band: 8 reviewer runs (59.00-59.87) and 6 orchestrator runs at load average 3.19 (58.97-59.22), plus the orchestrator's own committed gate run (59.15) — ~15 runs, none over 60, against the published 60.44 and 60.59. Asked to substantiate the two outliers as loaded-machine runs before dropping them, the repair ran 7 more: 6 at load average 2.3-4.9 (58.97-59.41) and one deliberately under artificial load — 8 CPU-pinned `yes` processes, load average driven to 8.4 on a 14-core machine — which measured 58.96s, at the low end rather than the high end of the range. Heavy concurrent CPU load did not reproduce a slowdown, let alone push the suite over 60s: this suite's wall clock is dominated by fixed sleeps and timeout bounds, not CPU contention, so 'busy machine' does not explain the two outliers and they are dropped as unsubstantiated. Across three independent measurers, ~22 runs, idle and deliberately loaded alike, land at 58.96-59.87s; a published band presented as an unconditioned measurement had two runs nobody else — including a dedicated attempt to reproduce them under load — could reproduce. `WALL_BUDGET_S` reverted to 60 on that evidence. (7) The revert commit's own claim — headroom ~0.13s against a max reproducible run of 59.87 — did not survive its own verification: 21 further real (non-stubbed) runs against the reverted, committed tree found the honest band is 58.83-60.26s, and the very first of those 21 landed at 60.26s, over the just-reverted ceiling, at ordinary load with no concurrent stress. 20 of the next 21 stayed under 60. Combined with the earlier 22, three independent measurers now have 43 non-original-band runs against this tree: 42 under 60, 1 over, by 0.26s. `WALL_BUDGET_S` stays 60 on that weight of evidence (roughly 95-98% of runs, honestly counted, clear it, against the withdrawn band's claimed 71%), but the record states the residual openly rather than the falsely precise '~0.13s of headroom' the first revert shipped with — a claim that was itself falsified within the same review round it was written in, the same pattern this repo has recorded before: a declared limitation or guarantee gets demonstrated wrong within days, sometimes within the same sitting, and the fix is to say what is actually reproducible, not to round it to a cleaner number. (8) PR #29 R13: the ceiling finally became a coin flip on a commit that changed nothing but JSON — 60.24s against 60, 109/109 passing. M31 had added real cost and the first repair moved three browser cases to `invariant`-only tags instead of facing it, which took ~4.9s out of the measured number and left the gate non-deterministic while the published `fast` figure stayed at 59.7s. ADR-019 amends Decision 4: the three cases are back in `fast`, the local ceiling is re-measured to 75 by this ADR's own rule (slowest observed +15%, rounded up to a multiple of five), and `invariant` gets a ceiling of its own at 15 so a tag can never again be an unbounded relief valve. This case grades both suites now, despite its id — the `suites_with_a_ceiling` set check is what makes a third suite appearing without a number turn it red, and the new `invariant_override` rows pin that CI's EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S=80 does not raise invariant's. (9) PR #29 R15/R19: the `invariant` ceiling added in (8) was derived from local runs and enforced only on CI, where it had never been measured — CI went red at 15.06s and 15.22s with 46/46 passing, and `.githooks/pre-commit` runs `fast` alone so nothing local could ever catch it. The override is now one variable per suite (`EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S_FAST`, `EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S_INVARIANT`), which is the symmetry ADR-013 Decision 3 already ruled `fast` needed, and both CI numbers are measured on CI: four attempts of commit d173340 gave invariant 14.80-16.47s and fast 69.37-74.06s, so 20 and 90. The old CI `fast` ceiling of 80 was the next coin flip at 8% margin against a 6.8% runner spread. (10) PR #29 R21: both local numbers were derived from bands that did not match the ledger committed beside them — `fast`'s published maximum (64.71s) was in no recorded run and the true maximum was 65.14s, and `invariant`'s band published five of sixteen runs and dropped the two slowest, so its ceiling was 15 where the rule had always said 20 (13.57 x 1.15 = 15.6). Both are re-derived from every run the ledger records at the shipped case count — `fast` 65.53 x 1.15 = 75.4 -> 80, `invariant` 14.12 x 1.15 = 16.2 -> 20 — and `published-band-matches-the-ledger` now grades that property on every run so prose cannot drift from the ledger again. (9) The local `fast` ceiling moved 80 -> 90 (ADR-021), on the number `published-band-matches-the-ledger` derives rather than one anybody chose: at 146 cases the committed ledger's slowest run is 74.77s and ADR-013's rule gives 90, which the grader reported as `required_by_adr013_rule` while the committed ceiling was still 80. Every 80 in this case was the local ruling and moves with it; `invariant` stays 20, because 54 cases still derive 20. The 89.62s row moved with the ceiling rather than being deleted: it is a real recorded CI run and it was `over` against 60 and against 80, and is not against 90. Missing it on the first pass of the ADR-021 edit is exactly the drift this case exists to catch, and it caught it — a boundary case whose rows are only the boundary itself would not have. M43 (ADR-035 Decision 7) moved the local `fast` ceiling 105 -> 110 on the ledger's slowest run at 238 cases (93.44s, ts `20260827-212200`; PR #70's repair round added two cases and the same rule returned the same 110, which is why two copies of the superseded 236-case row survived a round unnoticed — R8), and this case's boundary rows move with it — the 105.0/105.01 pair became 110.0/110.01 and every env_override default that reads the committed number went with them. That coupling is the point: a ceiling raised in evals/run.py and not here would leave the boundary graded at the old number. ADR-039 moved the local `fast` ceiling 110 -> 115 and then the same rule moved it back: at 241 cases every run measures ~94.9s, which derives 110. The raise and its withdrawal are both in ADR-019 §2. The rows here are at 110 for that reason, not because the raise never happened. ADR-039 moves the local `fast` ceiling 110 -> 115 on the ledger's slowest run at 241 cases (96.99s, ts `20260828-083202`), and this case's boundary rows move with it: the 110.0/110.01 pair became 115.0/115.01, every `env_override` default that reads the committed number went with them, and the far-side row moved 120 -> 130 because a row five seconds over a ceiling is a boundary row, not the unambiguous over-budget case that slot exists to hold. The number was published as 110 for one commit-in-progress on a two-run band (94.95s, 94.92s) and the third run at the same count measured 96.99s — a short sample presented as settled, falsified immediately, which is why `published-band-matches-the-ledger` reads the MAXIMUM. `ci_wall_seconds` stays 140: CI's number is measured on CI and nothing here re-measured it. Then back to 110, and the round trip is the record: ADR-039's later cases took the count to 242, five runs at that count span 94.81-95.63s, and 95.63 x 1.15 = 109.97 -> 110. Every band this milestone published on two or three samples was falsified by the next run, in BOTH directions — which is the argument for the maximum rule and against anyone's summary of a short sample, including this sentence's. Settled at 115 on six samples at 242 cases spanning 94.81-96.70s. The 110 above was published on five of those six; the sixth was run to confirm it and refuted it. Five bands, four falsifications, one session — the boundary rows here move with the committed number every time, which is the coupling this case exists for. Final state for this milestone: 115, on five samples at 243 cases spanning 94.96-95.76s. The number was published SEVEN times in one session as each short sample was falsified by the next run. The boundary rows here moved with it every time, which is the coupling this case exists for and also the clearest argument that a band needs more samples than the width of the distribution it summarises. ADR-039 moves BOTH local ceilings — `fast` 115 -> 120 on the ledger's slowest run at 253 cases (101.24s, ts `20260828-113600`) and `invariant` 35 -> 40 at 103 cases (31.87s, ts `20260828-113017`) — and every boundary row here moves with them, which is the coupling this case exists for. Unlike the previous moves on these lines it is not purely case-count growth: four cases entered `fast` and two `invariant`, and the rest is per-case cost from ADR-039 §1's settle, with ADR-021's waste-removal step done first and measured (7.3s regression, 4.8s returned by narrowing to fetch/xhr, 0.25s by the poll tick). `ci_wall_seconds` and `ci_invariant_wall_seconds` are untouched: CI's numbers are measured on CI and this branch has no CI runs of its own tree. T-R21 (P2) and T-R74 (P1) close here 2026-08-28. T-R21: the `or over_budget(args.suite, totals["wall_seconds"])` clause in `red` decides whether a full per-case report is written, and no case could observe it because every `applied_in_main` probe passed `--no-report` — so deleting the clause reddened nothing. `_main_exit_code` grew a `want_report` mode that drops the flag and returns what appeared in the temp report dir; two rows now pin both directions (green run writes nothing, over-budget run writes a report AND exits 1). The evidence for a wall-clock failure IS the timing, so a run that dies on it with no artifact is the one shape where the failure cannot be read afterwards. T-R74: that CI tags its rows `ci` is what keeps a CI row out of a `local` band, and it was asserted rather than demonstrated; this case already parses the workflow for its two ceiling declarations, so it now also pins that the workflow declares an environment and that it is not `local`. Ceiling named: it grades the DECLARATION, not that Actions sets `CI` and not that the tag survives into a committed row — that half needs a CI artifact and stays T-R73's. T-M39-2's SECOND symptom closes here too, graded behaviourally rather than by grepping the source: the probe reads the row `main()` actually wrote into its temp ledger and requires the `judge_usd` KEY. Its value is 0.0 on a stubbed run and that is fine — what was wrong is that the key did not exist, so a committed row could not answer "what did this run cost" for the half of the spend the judge accounts for. `cost_usd` deliberately keeps meaning PLANNER spend: every one of the ~2500 rows already written means that, and redefining a field in place makes old and new rows silently incomparable, which is the drift this ledger exists to make impossible.

triage.note: grades a rule and the place it is applied, because holes have appeared at both. `_main_exit_code` drives the real `evals.run.main()` with `load_cases`/`run_case` stubbed to a single result of a chosen duration — no case runs, no report is written, stdout and stderr are swallowed — so what is graded is the value `main()` RETURNS. One line short of the path CI takes: `evals/run.py`'s `if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())` tail is what turns that value into a process exit code, `_main_exit_code` calls `main()` in-process and never goes through it, and changing the tail to a bare `main()` would disable this ceiling — and the invariant and regression rules with it — with this case still green (PR #20 R13, Debt T-R13). The suite-key check is a set comparison rather than a row per suite name: rows can only ever cover the suites someone thought to list, and `full` was the one missing when `WALL_BUDGET_S["full"] = 1` was shown to slip through green (PR #20 R11). The env-override rows are all fallback except two, for the same reason: the dangerous direction is an override that quietly switches the gate off, not one that fails to apply. The override is one variable per suite as of ADR-019 (`EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S_FAST`, `EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S_INVARIANT`): one variable could not carry two suites' numbers, and scoping the single one to `fast` — the first attempt — left `invariant` unable to have a CI-measured number at all, which is how CI came to enforce a locally-derived 15s it had never run (PR #29 R15). CI's numbers are 90 and 20, measured on CI.
triage.not_covered: it grades total wall clock only — a case that gets 10s slower while another gets 10s faster is invisible to it; per-case timings are in every committed report for anyone looking. It does not drive `evals/run.py` as a process, so the module tail described above is ungraded. It does not exercise the `--update-baseline` path, which returns before the ceiling is consulted and reports nothing about it (PR #20 R12, Debt T-R12). Slower hardware is answered rather than uncovered: `EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S` gives an environment its own measured ceiling, and this case grades the override's fallbacks and the value the workflow declares — but nothing here checks that a declared number was ever measured. This case cannot tell a measured ceiling from an invented one; only an ADR-013 amendment with runs behind it can. It does not read a citation's body either: `adr-header-and-index` resolves the ADR references in this file — including the identifier spellings (`adr019`, `ADR_019`) that hid the fifth T-R52 miscitation, which was one of this case's own key names until PR #36 R4 — but only that the decision and any section it names exist, never that the decision rules on the subject (T-R57).
